extra_misconceptions.fact: Water conducts heat away from the body 25 times faster than air, so cold water causes rapid hypothermia even on hot sunny days.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Warm air temperatures above 80 degrees Fahrenheit eliminate the risk of hypothermia after a capsize in spring lake water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Low-head dams create a recirculating hydraulic backwash at the base that traps swimmers and kayaks underwater indefinitely.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Low-head dams are safe to paddle over because their vertical drop is usually only a few feet high.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rubbing cold extremities drives chilled blood back toward the heart and can trigger dangerous cardiac arrhythmias during recovery.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Vigorous arm and leg rubbing is the fastest way to rewarm a kayaker shivering from mild hypothermia.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Downwind cliffs reflect waves and block exits, so paddlers should land at a low protected shore immediately when thunder sounds.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Paddling close to a steep downwind shoreline provides the safest shelter when a thunderstorm approaches.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to your breathing reflex during the first minute of sudden immersion in water below 60 degrees Fahrenheit?
Why is it dangerous to paddle near a fallen tree strainer even when the surface current appears slow and calm?
Which physical indicator distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion when evaluating a tired paddler on shore?
What combined water and air temperature rule guides whether kayakers must wear thermal wetsuits or drysuits?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The swimmer test requires 75 yards of strong forward strokes followed specifically by 25 yards of an easy resting backstroke.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Completing 100 yards of fast freestyle swimming satisfies all parts of the Scouting America swimmer qualification test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every Scout must pass the full Swimmer classification test before attempting requirements 3 through 8 on the water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing a properly fitted life jacket allows a Beginner swimmer to participate solo in Kayaking merit badge lessons.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The entire 100-yard swim and subsequent floating rest must be completed continuously without touching the bottom or walls.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Touching the pool bottom or hanging on a lane line for five seconds is permitted between the 75-yard and 25-yard segments.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swim classifications must be renewed annually, and test administrators can retest any swimmer whose ability appears uncertain.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Passing the Scouting America swimmer test once as a new Scout remains valid until the Scout turns eighteen.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a paddler's energy reserves if they cannot transition into a resting backstroke after a long capsize swim?
Why is it dangerous to begin the Scouting America swimmer test with a shallow headfirst dive instead of a feetfirst jump?
What measurement confirms that a Scout has completed both the strong forward swim and the resting stroke segments?
Under what condition does a Scout need to renew their swimmer classification before participating in kayaking activities?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Safety Afloat requires every kayaker to wear a properly fitted life jacket at all times while on the water without exception.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stowing a Coast Guard approved life jacket under the deck bungees satisfies Scouting America rules on calm flatwater.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water swells or jams a cork pea inside the chamber, so kayakers must carry a pealess marine whistle clipped to their vest.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standard referee whistles with a cork pea inside work reliably for emergency signaling after a capsize.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must fasten all buckles and cinch the lower waist straps first so the vest anchors below your ribcage during immersion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tightening only the top chest buckle keeps a paddling life jacket from riding up over your chin in the water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A paddle float slides over one paddle blade to create an outrigger stabilizer across the stern deck during solo self-rescue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Inflatable paddle floats are worn around the paddler's wrists to help them swim back to shore after losing a boat.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that your kayaking life jacket fits snugly when a buddy pulls upward on the shoulder straps?
Where should a Scout position a pealess whistle so it remains reachable immediately after an unexpected capsize?
Why is it dangerous to rely solely on a foam sponge instead of a manual bilge pump after a deep-water re-entry?
Which structural features make a Type III paddling vest better suited for kayak strokes than a bulky Type I offshore vest?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heavy rocker and short hull length make whitewater kayaks pivot rapidly, whereas long touring hulls with minimal rocker track straight.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Short, wide whitewater kayaks with heavy rocker track in a straight line better than long, narrow touring kayaks.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ultraviolet rays degrade plastic resins and heat softens the hull, causing flat spots called oil-canning unless stored shaded on edge.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving a plastic kayak flat on hot concrete in direct summer sunlight preserves its original hull shape.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Elastic deck rigging only secures light gear and will snap or tear out deck fittings if used to lift the weight of a kayak.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carrying a waterlogged kayak by its elastic deck bungees is just as safe as lifting it by the bow and stern toggles.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Flat hulls stay level until tilted past their chine limit, while rounded hulls offer strong secondary stability in rough side waves.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flat-bottomed kayaks with high primary stability are more stable in steep breaking side waves than rounded touring hulls.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a kayak's straight-line tracking and turning radius when designers increase hull rocker from bow to stern?
Which hull characteristic determines whether a kayak feels steady on flat water versus remaining stable when leaned on edge?
Why is it dangerous to paddle a recreational kayak without sealed bulkheads or flotation bags far from shore?
Where should a Scout position support straps or padded racks when storing a polyethylene kayak for the winter?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only your dominant control hand maintains a fixed grip to rotate the shaft, while the opposite hand opens slightly so it can pivot.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Both hands should grip the paddle shaft tightly and spin it equally when paddling with feathered blades.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fine sand and salt crystals corrode or seize the ferrule joint unless you separate and rinse both shaft halves after every trip.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Storing a two-piece kayak paddle assembled all season prevents wear on the center ferrule locking pin.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Arm-only paddling fatigues small shoulder muscles quickly, whereas torso rotation engages large core and back muscles for sustained power.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling the paddle shaft exclusively with your biceps generates more forward speed than rotating your torso.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The concave spooned power face catches water cleanly during forward strokes, while the convex back face slices through on recovery.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The convex rounded back face of an asymmetric kayak blade should pull against the water during forward strokes.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that your hands are spaced properly on the paddle shaft before taking a forward stroke?
Where should a Scout position the drip rings on the paddle shaft to keep water from running down onto their hands?
What happens to the upper blade's wind resistance when you feather a two-piece paddle and rotate with your control hand?
Why is it dangerous to jam your paddle tip against submerged rocks to push a grounded kayak off a gravel bar?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swimming or treading water flushes cold water past your groin and armpits, accelerating core heat loss by more than 35 percent.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Treading water vigorously keeps your core warmer in cold water than floating still in the HELP position.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaning backward traps your knees under the deck, so you must tuck forward first and push your hips straight out of the cockpit.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: During a wet exit, you should kick your feet out of the cockpit before leaning forward or releasing the coaming.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pulling downward on one side flips both kayaks, so swimmers must stay low on their chest across the rear deck before sliding feet in.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Climbing upright onto the side coaming like a pool ladder is the most stable way to reenter a kayak in deep water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An upright flooded kayak weighs hundreds of pounds, so keep it inverted while sliding the bow across your cockpit to drain the hull.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Flipping a swamped kayak upright in the water before lifting its bow onto your deck makes a T-rescue easier.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position their body relative to a capsized kayak when swimming it toward shore in moving water?
What happens to the rescuer's fingers if they grab the victim's bow toggle while lifting the boat for a T-rescue?
Which high-heat-loss body areas does the Heat Escape Lessening Posture protect while waiting for rescue in cold water?
Under what condition does a swimmer flip an emptied kayak back upright during a kayak-over-kayak rescue?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Continuing a forward stroke past your hip pulls the stern downward and turns the bow, so slice the blade out right at your hip.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling the forward stroke blade all the way past your hip to the stern increases your kayak's forward speed.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A forward sweep uses a low horizontal shaft angle and traces a wide arc from bow to stern to maximize turning leverage.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Forward sweep strokes use the same close-to-the-hull vertical shaft angle as a standard forward propulsion stroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Prying against the hull pushes the kayak backward, so rotate your wrist 90 degrees before touching the boat to slice the blade back out.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Prying the paddle shaft off the side coaming is the safest way to recover your blade between draw strokes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Keep your normal grip and push the back face of the blade from your hip toward the bow so you can switch strokes immediately.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Spinning the paddle 180 degrees in your hands is required before executing a stopping backstroke.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position the paddle blade exit point during a forward stroke to avoid lifting water at the stern?
What happens to the kayak's bow direction when you execute a wide forward sweep on the left side of the hull?
Why is it dangerous to leave the submerged paddle blade locked in the water at the end of a side draw stroke?
Which blade path distinguishes a turning stern draw from a pure sideways draw stroke next to your hip?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Alternating a forward sweep on one side with a reverse sweep on the other pivots the hull around its center within one boat length.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Paddling with only forward sweeps on one side spins a kayak 180 degrees in place without forward drift.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Braking on only one side spins the bow violently, so alternate short, crisp backstrokes on both sides to stop in a straight line.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Holding a single long braking stroke on one side stops a moving kayak straight within one boat length.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pulling ahead of your center of gravity rotates the bow, so plant the draw blade directly abeam of your hip for pure sideways motion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing the draw blade closer to the bow than your hip moves the kayak straight abeam for 10 feet.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Centrifugal force pushes a turning kayak toward the outside, so edge the hull with your knees while keeping your head centered over it.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaning your upper body toward the inside of a sharp buoy turn increases kayak stability around a figure-eight course.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a kayak's directional control in a crosswind when heavy gear makes the hull trim bow-down?
Which combination of strokes spins a stationary kayak 180 degrees in place without drifting outside two boat lengths?
Where should a Scout position their gaze and torso while paddling backward for four boat lengths in a straight line?
Under what condition does a kayak turn rather than glide straight sideways during a 10-foot abeam draw maneuver?
